chapter_theme: Folly as choosing loss over gain. It is not ignorance as such: its worst form belongs to the learned who do not restrain themselves, and it spoils whatever the fool touches, whether work, wealth, friendship or an assembly.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: its definition (831-832), the fool's conduct in general (833-834), his fate after death (835), how he gets and uses wealth (836-838), his friendship (839), and his place in an assembly (840).

831.reading: What is the one thing called folly? It is taking hold of harm and letting gain go.
831.nuance: This is a definition by behaviour rather than by lack of knowledge. Parimelazhagar lists poverty, blame and sin as the harm and wealth, fame and virtue as the gain, so he reads the choice as ruining both worlds.

832.reading: Of all follies the worst is to set one's love on what is not for one's hand.

positions.position: It means conduct forbidden by the treatises, loved and done anyway.
positions.quote: இருமைக்கும் ஆகாதென்று நூலோர் கடிந்த செயல்களை விரும்பிச் செய்தல் என்பதாம்.

positions.position: It means something out of reach, loved even though effort won't get it.
It means tasks beyond one's ability, and meddling in them.
positions.quote: தன்னால் இயலாத செயல்களை விரும்பி, அவற்றில் தலையிடுவது

833.reading: No shame, no searching, no tenderness, no care for anything: this is what a fool does.
833.nuance: The fool is described by four absences, in a chain of words ending in -மை. தொழில் suggests something habitual: Parimelazhagar says these are his constant nature. நார் is a fibre, a bond, and also fellow-feeling.

834.reading: There is no greater fool than one who studies, understands and teaches others but does not restrain himself.
834.nuance: All three stages of learning are granted, and restraint alone is missing. Parimelazhagar makes it medical: this folly isn't cured by its own remedy, and no other remedy exists.

835.reading: A fool can, in one life's doing, make the mire he will enter and sink into for seven.

positions.position: The mire is hell, and all future births are lived in hell's suffering because of one life's cruel deeds.
positions.quote: வரும் பிறவிகள் எல்லாம் தான் புக்கு அழுந்தும் நிரயத்தினை

positions.position: ஒருமை is acting on one's own whim, and எழுமை simply means always. The mire is suffering with no births or hell involved.
positions.quote: எக் காலத்திலும் துன்பமெனும் சகதியில் அழுந்திக் கிடக்க நேரிடும்.

836.reading: If a fool who doesn't know how takes up a task, it comes to nothing, and more than that, he wears fetters.
836.nuance: பூணும் is what one does with jewellery, so the fetters are worn like ornaments. Manakkudavar takes பொய்படும் to mean he himself gets called false, whereas Parimelazhagar means the work collapses inside.

837.reading: When a fool gets great wealth, strangers feast and his own people go hungry.
837.nuance: The verse says உற்றக்கடை, 'when it has come to him'. Parimelazhagar takes this as wealth got by fate, on the argument that a fool couldn't have made it himself. The next verse's பெறின் gets the same treatment. Both are his additions.

838.reading: When a fool gets something into his hand, it is like a man already deranged getting drunk.
838.nuance: The image is of something added to an existing state. Wealth doesn't produce the folly but compounds it, and ஒன்று, 'some one thing', suggests it doesn't take much.

839.reading: The friendship of fools is very sweet, for there is nothing painful about parting from them.
839.nuance: பிரிவு is a word that carries great weight in the Book of Love, so the 'sweetness' measured by painless parting reads like the opposite of what love is.

positions.position: It is mock praise, blame dressed as praise: the friendship wanes daily, so parting hurts no one.
It concerns women's relations with foolish men, and how a fool enjoys desire.
He gives the literal sense, with no irony marked: it is sweet because parting brings no sorrow.

840.reading: A fool's entering an assembly of the worthy is like placing an unwashed foot on a bed.
840.nuance: The harm passes to the place: the bed and the assembly are both defiled, not the foot or the fool. Parimelazhagar notes that 'unwashed' is a polite cover for what the foot has trodden, which Kalaignar spells out.

links.note: A precise inversion using the same ஒருமை and எழுமை. In 398 learning gained in one birth protects for seven. In 835 folly done in one birth drowns for seven. One life's leverage on all the lives to come works in both directions.

823 says study doesn't reform the hostile. 834 turns the same point on the student and teacher himself: he is the worst fool. Learning fails as moral change in both, first in the other and then in oneself.
782 says a fool's friendship wanes like the moon. Parimelazhagar uses that waning to explain 839's joke: because it has been shrinking every day, by the time of parting nothing is left to hurt.

source_issues: 837: Parimelazhagar's word-gloss opens with a misprint, பதை for பேதை.
